summaries.example: Imagine a joke that starts, “I opened my lunchbox and found a…” You expect food. The ending says, “a tiny piano!” Your expectation is changed suddenly. That surprise may make you laugh. But if the surprise were frightening or hurtful, you might not laugh. This shows why surprise alone may not be enough for humor.
summaries.summary: Philosophy asks what humor is, why people laugh, and whether humor is good or bad. For a long time, many philosophers focused on laughter that mocked people or showed a loss of self-control. Three important explanations are the superiority theory, the relief theory, and the incongruity theory. Superiority theory says laughter shows that we feel above someone. Relief theory says laughter releases built-up tension. Incongruity theory says humor comes from a mismatch between expectation and experience, such as a punch line that changes the meaning of a joke. Each theory explains some humor but has limits. The entry gives special attention to humor as play: people safely bend ordinary ways of speaking and thinking for enjoyment. Laughter can signal that the play is not a real fight or serious attack. Humor may help with rest, friendship, flexible thinking, and seeing problems from a wider angle. Still, jokes can be unkind or harmful, especially when they repeat unfair stereotypes or make light of something that deserves serious care. Comedy and philosophy can be alike because both question familiar ideas and look at ordinary life in surprising ways.
key_ideas: People often value humor, but many older philosophers criticized laughter, especially mocking or uncontrolled laughter.
The superiority theory connects laughter with feeling above someone else, but it cannot explain every case, such as laughing at wordplay or at your own mistake.
The relief theory says laughter releases pressure. The entry describes this idea but notes that its old picture of the nervous system has serious problems.
The incongruity theory says humor involves a surprising mismatch with our usual expectations. Many philosophers and psychologists think this explains a lot, but not every surprise is funny.
A newer approach treats humor as play. Play can help people relax, think flexibly, and connect with others, while still needing good judgment.
summaries.why_it_matters: Humor is part of everyday life, friendships, stories, and public conversation. Thinking about it helps us notice why a joke works, why people disagree about what is funny, and why context matters. Humor can bring rest and connection, but it is not automatically harmless. Learning to enjoy playful surprises while noticing when someone is being hurt is an important kind of good judgment.

important_terms.definition: A way of explaining something. Philosophers compare different theories to see what each one explains well and what problems it has.
A surprising mismatch between what we expect and what happens or between ideas that do not seem to fit together.
Fun activity done without treating it like a serious task. Humor can be a kind of thinking and talking play.
The idea that laughter comes from feeling above someone else, or above an earlier version of yourself.
The idea that laughter lets out built-up pressure or tension. The entry explains why many current scholars do not accept this as a full explanation.
A sign that tells people an action is playful rather than serious. Smiling and laughing can work this way.

questions_to_think_about: Can you think of a time you laughed without feeling better than anyone else?
Is every surprising thing funny? Why might a surprise make someone scared instead?
When can a joke help people feel close, and when might it hurt someone?
Why might making mistakes seem funny in a safe situation but not in a dangerous one?

summaries.example: A joke says, “I love visiting museums. They have so many works of art—especially the ones that are still working.” The word “works” first suggests art objects, then shifts toward things functioning. The amusement comes from an incongruity in language and from resolving the shift. No feeling of superiority is required, and there is no obvious burst of emotion that had to be released. Yet the joke is not funny merely because it is unusual: a disturbing or disgusting mismatch may produce fear or anger instead. The audience’s attitude and the context matter.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of humor examines a topic that people commonly value but that received surprisingly little sustained philosophical attention for much of Western history. Older criticism often treated laughter as scornful, uncontrolled, or morally risky. The entry organizes major explanations around the superiority, relief, and incongruity theories. Superiority theory links amusement to a comparative rise in self-esteem, but counterexamples include wordplay, laughter at one’s own present mistake, and admiration for a comic performer’s skill. Relief theory describes laughter as the discharge of energy no longer needed for emotion, thought, or inhibition. Its historical versions are influential, especially Freud’s, but the entry emphasizes problems with both the outdated physiological picture and several psychological assumptions. Incongruity theory identifies a mismatch between expectation and experience, or between a concept and a particular case. It is more inclusive, but incongruity alone can be frightening, offensive, or aesthetically disturbing rather than funny. Some theorists add incongruity-resolution; others argue that resolution does not characterize every form of humor. The entry’s constructive proposal understands humor as cognitive and social play. Humor temporarily suspends ordinary practical seriousness, allowing people to manipulate language and ideas, gain distance from problems, and interact with others. Laughter can function as a play signal, possibly rooted in the mock-aggressive play of ancestral apes. Humor may support flexibility, social ease, and coping, but ethical judgment remains necessary because jokes can reinforce stereotypes or make serious suffering harder to recognize. Comedy, like philosophy, can question authority, examine ordinary life,‍
key_ideas: The entry surveys three traditional theories. Superiority theory explains mocking laughter but struggles with self-laughter, wordplay, and cases where the audience admires rather than surpasses the comic figure.
Relief theory treats laughter as the release of energy or tension. Historical versions differ, but the entry notes that contemporary scholars rarely use the hydraulic model as a general explanation.
Incongruity theory is prominent because humor often involves violated expectations, conflicting interpretations, or a mismatch between concepts and particular things.

Incongruity by itself is insufficient: the same violation can produce amusement, fear, disgust, pity, or anger. Some accounts therefore add enjoyment, a playful attitude, or a successful resolution of the mismatch.
The play approach explains why humor may be socially useful. It lets people experiment with language, expectations, and perspectives without treating the activity as an ordinary serious action.
The evolutionary discussion proposes that laughter may have developed from play signals connected with mock-aggressive play. This is presented as a hypothesis, not a settled history of humor.
summaries.why_it_matters: Humor provides a test case for how emotion, reasoning, language, social interaction, aesthetics, and morality fit together. Its study also challenges the assumption that rational thought must always be solemn. Playful departures from ordinary expectations can reveal hidden assumptions and create social connection, but disengagement is not always appropriate. The philosophical issue is therefore not simply whether humor is good or bad; it is how different forms of humor work, what attitudes they require, and what effects they have in particular contexts.

important_terms.definition: An account proposed to explain a phenomenon. The entry compares theories partly by asking what kinds of humor they can explain and what cases challenge them.
A mismatch between mental patterns, concepts, or expectations and what is perceived or experienced. In humor, this mismatch is typically enjoyed rather than merely noticed.
The view that amusement or laughter expresses a sudden sense of superiority over another person or over one’s former condition.
The view that laughter discharges excess nervous or psychic energy produced by emotion, thought, or psychological restraint. The entry presents historical versions and major objections.
The view that humor is a form of non-serious, enjoyable activity in which people exercise cognitive and social abilities in unusual ways.
A smile, laugh, or similar behavior that marks an activity as playful rather than as genuine aggression or another serious action.
A genre that represents conflicts and incongruities through comic rather than tragic responses. The entry contrasts comedy’s pragmatic, anti-heroic stance with tragedy’s serious engagement.

The position that moral defects in a joke or comic performance can affect its aesthetic success. Philosophers disagree about whether immoral features always reduce amusement, sometimes increase it, or do neither in a simple way.

questions_to_think_about: Does resolving a confusing punch line explain all humor, or only some jokes?
Can a person enjoy an incongruity without finding it amusing? What examples support your answer?
How might laughter communicate that teasing or mock aggression is playful?
Should a joke’s moral content affect how funny it is? Consider audience, context, and possible social effects.
In what ways do philosophy and stand-up comedy both make familiar experiences seem strange?

summaries.example: Suppose a friend asks why you forgot to bring your part of a group project. You answer, “I was busy training my goldfish for the Olympics.” The answer breaks the normal rule that a reply should be relevant and truthful. It is also obviously playful. The joke works because the group recognizes the mismatch between the serious question and the impossible excuse. If your friend had really lost the project or was upset, the same joke might seem rude instead of funny.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of humor asks what makes things funny, why laughter happens, and whether humor improves or damages human life. Although people often say humor is important, older philosophers wrote relatively little about it and frequently treated laughter with suspicion. They especially worried about scorn, cruelty, and loss of self-control. The entry examines three traditional theories. The superiority theory says we laugh when we feel above someone else or above a previous version of ourselves. That may explain mocking laughter, but not many examples of wordplay, self-mockery, or admiration. The relief theory says laughter releases energy created by suspense, emotion, or mental effort. Historical thinkers developed different versions, but the entry explains why current scholars generally do not use the old pressure model as a complete explanation. The incongruity theory says humor involves a clash with expectations, such as a punch line that changes how we understand the beginning of a joke. Some accounts emphasize solving or reinterpreting the mismatch. Still, incongruity can also be frightening or upsetting, so amusement involves more than surprise. The entry then develops the idea that humor is play. In humor, people can safely bend ordinary conversation rules and try unusual ways of thinking. Laughter may act as a signal that the activity is playful rather than genuinely aggressive. This approach helps explain possible benefits of humor, including rest, social connection, and mental flexibility. It also leaves room for moral concerns: jokes may repeat stereotypes or treat serious suffering too lightly. Comedy and philosophy share a habit of examining familiar life from a surprising distance.
key_ideas: Many earlier thinkers distrusted humor because they associated it with mockery, bad behavior, or losing self-control.
The superiority theory fits some insulting jokes, but it does not explain every laugh. People can laugh at puns, unexpected objects, clever escapes, or their own mistakes.

The relief theory says laughter lowers pressure after suspense or emotion. The entry discusses historical versions, but says few scholars now accept the old energy-release picture as a complete account.
The incongruity theory focuses on surprises and mismatches. It is influential because jokes often set up one expectation and then switch to another.
A surprising mismatch is not automatically humorous. It might instead cause fear, disgust, sadness, or anger. Humor usually involves enjoying the mismatch in a suitable setting.
The play view presents humor as a safe way to experiment with thinking and social interaction. It can support relaxation, flexible problem-solving, and relationships, but jokes can also cause harm.
summaries.why_it_matters: Humor affects friendships, classrooms, entertainment, and public discussion. Understanding its theories helps explain why the same joke can delight one audience and offend another. It also shows that humor is not merely a silly extra: it can involve reasoning, language, emotions, and social signals. At the same time, enjoying a joke does not settle whether the joke is fair or helpful. Good judgment includes knowing when playful distance is useful and when compassion or serious action is needed.

important_terms.definition: An organized explanation of why something happens. Philosophers compare theories by looking at the examples each can explain and the examples that cause trouble.
A mismatch between what we expect and what we notice, or between ideas that normally do not belong together.
The claim that laughter comes from feeling higher, smarter, safer, or more successful than another person or an earlier version of yourself.
The claim that laughter releases built-up mental or bodily tension, like pressure leaving a container. The entry says this approach has important weaknesses.
A way of understanding humor as enjoyable, non-serious activity. People play with words, ideas, and social rules while signaling that they are not acting completely seriously.
A behavior that tells others, “This is play, not a real attack or serious action.” Laughter and smiling can serve this purpose.
The organized comic form that developed in ancient Greece and is often contrasted with tragedy. Comedy can show practical, flexible responses to life’s problems.
A judgment about whether humor is morally acceptable or harmful. A joke can be playful without being harmless, especially if it repeats damaging stereotypes.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the superiority theory explain some teasing but not every kind of laughter?
What is the difference between finding something surprising and finding it funny?
How can laughter help people know that rough behavior is only pretend?
Can a joke be funny and still be morally troubling? Explain with a situation.
Why might comedy and philosophy both question ordinary assumptions?
